extracted.intended_audience: readers and researchers interested in 19th–early 20th century sailing ships, maritime historians, shipping enthusiasts
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the metrics, measurements, and narrative criteria used in the historical account to judge the performance, condition, and fate of clippers and similar sailing ships (e.g., passage times, spar plans, cargo fit, sea-handling).

rubrics_metrics.name: Passage duration / passage times
rubrics_metrics.description: Elapsed days from departure to arrival (e.g., 'Days Out' in the 'Passages under 80 Days' tables).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a primary performance metric to compare ships (examples: 68 days, 75 days, under-80 lists). Tables list departure point, crossings (equator, Cape meridian), passed Cape Otway/S.W. Cape Tasmania, arrival and total days. Frequently used to identify 'maiden voyage' records and to compare contemporaneous ships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Average passage performance / consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: A ship’s average passage times over a series of voyages (e.g., 'her average for 13 consecutive passages to Melbourne being 75 days').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Averages (outward/homeward) are used to judge overall reliability and sustained speed (examples: Salamis averages, Aristides regular passages 78–88 days). 'Best averages' cited as distinguishing ships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best 24‑hour run and multi‑day totals ('week’s work')
rubrics_metrics.description: Distance covered in a 24‑hour period or summed over several days (e.g., 'Loch Garry’s best run in the 24 hours was 333 miles', 'Loch Vennachar did a week’s work of 2065 miles').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to illustrate a ship’s peak performance capability and to validate claims of speed in narrative/logs (examples include daily runs of 300+ miles and seven‑day aggregates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermediate voyage milestones (equator, Cape meridian, Otway)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recorded dates/positions for crossing the equator, Cape meridian, passing Cape Otway/S.W. Cape Tasmania used as benchmarks during a passage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sequence and timing of these milestones appear in tabular logs and are used to compute legs of the voyage and day counts; they provide context for comparing different ships on the same route and year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registered tonnage and hull dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Official tonnage figures and principal dimensions (registered tonnage net/gross/under deck, length, breadth, depth, depth moulded) as recorded for ships (see Salamis vs Thermopylae table).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical size and tonnage are used to compare capacity and to relate size to speed and role (e.g., Salamis being roughly 100 tons larger and 10 feet longer than Thermopylae).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spar plan and mast/yard measurements
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed spar measurements (mast heights, mainyard and topsail yard lengths, jibboom length, doublings) as given in the 'SPAR PLAN OF SALAMIS'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These dimensions indicate sail-carrying ability and rig configuration; comparison of yard lengths and mast heights used to show Salamis 'set even more canvas than Thermopylae' and thus explain relative sailing power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sail plan / canvas area (including stunsails, flying kites)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent and type of canvas carried (stunsails, flying kites, spencers, skysails, hoisting spanker) and whether the ship was 'over canvassed' or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative links larger sail area or particular sails (e.g., Salamis’ 'tremendous sail plan', Harbinger's added 600 superficial feet) to speed potential; notes when stunsails were not fitted (limiting potential) or when spencer yards were present but unused (Cutty Sark).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction material and hull type (iron vs composite vs other)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the ship was iron-built or composite, and how that affected trade and voyages (e.g., Salamis as an 'iron Thermopylae', reference to iron ships occasionally topping 100 days).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction is presented as a factor in performance and trade suitability—iron ships had differing average speeds and trade placements compared with composite/wood clippers, and some records explicitly compare iron and composite sister ships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loading, trim, and stowage (Plimsoll marks, deep/lean loading)
rubrics_metrics.description: How carefully a ship is loaded, with specific note of 'Plimsoll marks well out of water' and loading depth affecting speed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful loading and not over-deep trim are cited as owner/firm practices (e.g., Aberdeen White Star) that helped secure fast maiden voyages; freight decisions (e.g., low freights at Shanghai) also affected which trades ships entered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crew quality and captain competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of captains and crews ('crews also were picked men', named captains associated with ships’ reputations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Named captains and the practice of selecting experienced/skilled crews are invoked as important determinants of achieving record passages and handling difficult weather; examples include Captain Phillip, Captain Kemball, Captain Davidson, Captain Largie, Captain Hunter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sea‑handling qualities and vessel behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualitative descriptions of how a ship handles at sea (stiffness, docility, ability to 'stay', steer in light airs, how she parts the waves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First‑hand testimony (e.g., Mr. Bullen on Harbinger) is used as evidence: ships that 'would stay under storm staysails' or 'steer when you could hardly detect an air' are judged superior for handling and safety as well as speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for passengers vs cargo (fitting and accommodations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a ship is fitted for passengers and the extent of passenger accommodation (e.g., Harbinger 'fitted to carry a large number of passengers', Salamis 'not fitted for passengers').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passenger fittings, accommodations, and related gear are noted to influence trade assignment and performance (passenger ships often had different rigging/gear and were slower if not hard‑pressed). Examples: Harbinger’s midship house and passenger capacity; Salamis’ short quarterdeck meant less passenger fitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modifications, repairs and their impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-damage repairs, alterations, or retrofits (e.g., Loch Vennachar raised and repaired to value of about £17,000; Harbinger had 600 superficial feet of canvas added; Norwegians stripped yards and converted to barque).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such changes are used to explain later performance, changes in trade, and longevity (repairs could restore condition to 'as good as the day she was launched'; conversions altered sailing characteristics and role).

rubrics_metrics.name: Voyage log extracts and positional records as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of captain’s log extracts (lat/long, daily distances, weather notes) as authoritative evidence of performance (e.g., detailed Harbinger log entries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logs provide day-by-day details (distances, wind, sail set, barometer) that support claims about runs, weather difficulty, and decision-making; often quoted to justify or contest reported speeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance variability under different wind conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements that a ship may be faster in light/moderate winds but not in strong winds (e.g., 'Sir Walter Raleigh was probably faster in light and moderate winds than in strong').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges that a ship’s comparative advantage can depend on wind regime; anecdotal and log evidence used to characterize these differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market/trade context affecting opportunities to demonstrate speed
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic and trade factors (e.g., steamers capturing the tea trade, slumping freights at Shanghai) that limited a clipper’s chance to carry lucrative fast cargoes like new teas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why fast ships sometimes failed to load tea cargoes and were relegated to other trades (wool, general cargo), thus altering both measured records and owners’ incentives to pursue speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incidents, collisions, wrecks and safety outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Recorded incidents (being run down by a steamer, collisions in fog, wrecked on rocks, man overboard) and resulting loss or survival of crew/passengers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as historical facts that mark a ship’s fate and affect reputational or operational assessment (examples: Loch Vennachar sunk then raised; Smyrna run into by steamer Moto; many ships 'lost with all hands' or 'never arrived'). Such incidents also provide context for loss-rates and risks of the era.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational practices aboard (sail handling, not 'hard sailing')
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of how a ship was normally handled (e.g., 'she was never hard sailed', 'never hove to in ten voyages') and implications for recorded times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational choices (pushing a ship hard vs conservative handling) are cited to explain why some ships with potential did not post extraordinary passages; logs and eyewitnesses note how aggressively ships were sailed.
